Capture a run

Codex exec and JSON Output

Run codex exec --json to capture one JSON event per line. Add -o to save the final assistant reply in a separate file. Before using the reply in another step, check the process exit code and the terminal event. Use --output-schema when the next step needs specific fields, then validate those fields.

  1. Capture events and the final reply
  2. Choose what to check
  3. Request and validate structured output
  4. Detect failed or incomplete runs
  5. Inspect tested examples

Capture events and the final reply

In your project directory, run a short read-only task. The example uses a fresh output directory and saves stderr separately. Keep real transcripts private because events can contain source text, file paths and tool output.

run_dir=$(mktemp -d)
status=0
codex exec --json --sandbox read-only -o "$run_dir/final.txt" \
  "Summarize the repo structure in one sentence." \
  > "$run_dir/events.jsonl" 2> "$run_dir/stderr.log" || status=$?
printf 'Codex exit: %s\n' "$status"

events.jsonl contains the event stream. Its completed agent_message item carries the reply. final.txt contains just the final message. A thread.started event carries the conversation ID for later use. See how to resume and verify that exact session.

Request a reply that follows a JSON Schema

Save the example schema in your current directory. It requires an object with one string field, result. Run a separate request with the schema file:

run_dir=$(mktemp -d)
status=0
codex exec --json --sandbox read-only --output-schema result.schema.json \
  -o "$run_dir/final.json" \
  "Give a one-sentence repo summary in the result field." \
  > "$run_dir/events.jsonl" 2> "$run_dir/stderr.log" || status=$?

Validate the reply before using it. In our loopback test, the CLI sent the schema. A test server deliberately ignored it and replied with {"result":17}. The CLI completed and wrote that reply. The downstream type check rejected it. This test covers the local CLI and a synthetic provider, and does not assess OpenAI model adherence.

Detect a failed or incomplete run

  1. Check the exit status from Codex. An item can finish before the run fails. In a shell pipeline, make sure you capture Codex’s status rather than only the last command’s status.
  2. Read the final turn state in the captured event file. A successful one-turn run should have turn.completed and a completed assistant message. Treat turn.failed or a cut-off stream as a failed check.
  3. When the next step needs structured data, check the field names and types after decoding the assistant message. A successful turn can still produce unusable data.

Download the Python check and run it on a single codex exec --json transcript. Pass the exit status from that run. The optional schema flag checks the one-field example above.

python3 check-run.py "$run_dir/events.jsonl" --exit-code "$status"
python3 check-run.py "$run_dir/events.jsonl" --exit-code "$status" --check-example-schema

Use the second command for the schema example. The check emits the thread ID and reply only after its checks pass. Adapt validation to your own schema for other outputs.
